stimuli.text: The graph of the function $$f$$ is shown. Open circles mark points not on the graph; closed dots mark function values.

image.alt: A line rising to an open circle at (1, 3.5) with a hole at (-2, 2); a closed dot at (1, 1); a downward parabola from x = 1 to 5 with an open circle at (3, 3) and a closed dot at (3, 0).

stimuli.text: A ball is dropped from a tall building. After $$t$$ seconds it has fallen $$s(t) = 16t^2$$ feet.

options.why: This is $$f(3)$$, the closed dot. The limit uses the values near 3, which approach 3.
Correct. The parabola approaches height 3 from both sides of $$x = 3$$.
This is $$f(1)$$, at a different input.
Both one-sided limits are 3, so the limit exists even though it differs from $$f(3)$$.

questions.explanation: Trace the curve toward $$x = 3$$ from each side: both approach the open circle at height 3. The closed dot at $$(3, 0)$$ gives $$f(3) = 0$$, which does not affect the limit.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about $$f$$ at $$x = 1$$ is true?

options.why: The right-hand limit is 1, but the left-hand limit is 3.5, so the two-sided limit does not exist.
From the left the line approaches the open circle at 3.5.
Correct. The left piece heads to 3.5 and the right piece starts at the closed dot, height 1.
The point at height 3.5 is an open circle, so it is not on the graph. The closed dot shows $$f(1) = 1$$.

questions.explanation: Approaching 1 from the left, the line rises toward 3.5. From the right, the parabola starts at height 1. The one-sided limits differ, so $$\lim_{x \to 1} f(x)$$ does not exist.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true at $$x = -2$$?

options.why: Correct. Both sides approach the open circle at height 2, and there is no closed dot at $$x = -2$$.
Both sides approach the same height, so the limit exists.
$$f(-2)$$ is undefined, so $$f$$ cannot be continuous there.
The open circle means the point is missing from the graph.

questions.explanation: The graph has a hole at $$(-2, 2)$$: the limit is 2, but $$f(-2)$$ is undefined. This is a removable discontinuity.

questions.stem: What is the average speed of the ball, in feet per second, from $$t = 1$$ to $$t = 3$$?

options.why: This is the distance fallen during the interval; divide by the 2 seconds that passed.
This is $$\frac{s(3)}{3}$$, which measures from $$t = 0$$, not from $$t = 1$$.
This is the instantaneous speed at $$t = 3$$, not the average over the interval.

questions.explanation: Average speed is change in distance over change in time: $$\frac{16(9) - 16(1)}{2} = 64$$ feet per second.

questions.stem: Average speeds over $$[2, 2.1]$$, $$[2, 2.01]$$ and $$[2, 2.001]$$ are 65.6, 64.16 and 64.016 feet per second. What is the best estimate of the ball's speed at the instant $$t = 2$$?

options.why: This is the average over the widest interval, the least accurate estimate.
This is the average speed from $$t = 0$$ to $$t = 2$$.
Correct. As the interval shrinks, the averages approach 64.

options.text: It cannot be found, because no time passes in an instant.
options.why: A limit of average speeds over shrinking intervals gives the instantaneous speed.

questions.explanation: The instantaneous speed is the limit of the average speeds as the interval shrinks. The values 65.6, 64.16, 64.016 approach 64 feet per second.

questions.stem: If $$\lim_{x \to 2} f(x) = 5$$ and $$\lim_{x \to 2} g(x) = -3$$, what is $$\lim_{x \to 2} \left[f(x)g(x) + 2f(x)\right]$$?

options.why: Correct. By the product, sum and constant multiple laws: $$5(-3) + 2(5) = -5$$.
This leaves out the $$2f(x)$$ term.
This adds the limits instead of multiplying them for the product term.
Sign error: $$2f(x)$$ contributes $$+10$$, not $$-10$$.

questions.explanation: Apply the limit laws term by term: $$\lim f(x)g(x) = 5 \cdot (-3) = -15$$ and $$\lim 2f(x) = 10$$, so the limit is $$-5$$.

questions.stem: If $$\lim_{x \to 4} f(x) = 6$$ and $$\lim_{x \to 4} g(x) = 0$$, which of the following must be true about $$\lim_{x \to 4} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)}$$?

options.why: The denominator, not the numerator, approaches 0.
Dividing by something approaching 0 does not leave the numerator unchanged.

options.text: It does not exist as a finite number.
options.why: Correct. A nonzero number divided by something approaching 0 grows without bound, so there is no finite limit.
The sign depends on how $$g$$ approaches 0, so the limit could be $$\infty$$, $$-\infty$$, or neither. It is certainly not finite.

questions.explanation: The quotient law needs a nonzero denominator limit. Here the numerator approaches 6 and the denominator approaches 0, so the quotient is unbounded near 4 and has no finite limit.
